raw_text:
# Cardiac Contractility Modulation Therapy for Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

Heart failure (HF) remains a major global public health challenge, associated with high morbidity, frequent hospitalizations, and substantial mortality despite guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) [1,2]. While device-based interventions such as cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) have significantly improved outcomes for patients with wide QRS complexes, approximately 70% of symptomatic HF patients present with a narrow QRS duration (<120 ms) and are thus ineligible for CRT [3,4]. Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) has emerged as a promising, innovative device-based therapy designed specifically to address this therapeutic gap in patients with symptomatic HF who remain limited despite optimal medical management [5,6]. First investigated in clinical trials in the early 2000s [7,8], CCM has transitioned from a novel concept to an established, guideline-supported therapeutic option [1,2].

## Mechanism of Action

Unlike pacemakers or CRTs that deliver excitatory electrical impulses to initiate myocardial contraction, CCM delivers high-voltage, non-excitatory electrical signals during the absolute refractory period of the cardiac cycle [9,10]. Because these signals are timed during the refractory phase, they do not trigger ectopic beats or arrhythmias, but instead exert profound effects on myocardial biology at both the cellular and molecular levels [11,12]. 

The primary immediate mechanism of CCM involves the modulation of intracellular calcium ($Ca^{2+}$) handling [13]. At the cellular level, CCM signal delivery rapidly enhances calcium influx through L-type calcium channels and restores the activity of the sarcoplasmic reticulum $Ca^{2+}$-ATPase 2a (SERCA2a) and phospholamban phosphorylation [11,13]. This restores sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium loading and subsequent calcium release during systole, enhancing contractile force [11,13]. 

Over the long term, chronic CCM therapy triggers a molecular reverse remodeling process [14]. It normalizes the expression of key proteins involved in calcium handling and downregulates the "fetal gene program" characteristic of heart failure [11,13]. Crucially, while these signals are delivered locally to the right ventricular septum, their molecular and functional benefits rapidly propagate, leading to global improvements in left ventricular (LV) contractility and reverse remodeling without a concomitant increase in myocardial oxygen consumption [15,16].

## Clinical Trial Evidence and Efficacy

The safety and efficacy of CCM have been established in multiple randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Early clinical studies validated the acute hemodynamic benefits and safety of the therapy [7,9,16,17]. The pivotal FIX-HF-5 trial randomized 412 patients with NYHA class III/IV HF and left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) between 12% and 35% to CCM or optimal medical therapy [18]. While the study's primary efficacy endpoint of anaerobic threshold did not reach statistical significance in the overall cohort, a pre-specified subgroup analysis identified patients with LVEF $\ge$ 25% and NYHA class III symptoms as high responders [19].

This led to the design of the FIX-HF-5C trial, which targeted this specific responder population (LVEF 25%–45%, NYHA class III/IV, QRS < 120 ms) [20]. FIX-HF-5C demonstrated a significant improvement in functional capacity, as measured by peak oxygen consumption ($pVO_2$) and the 6-minute hall walk distance (6MWD), alongside a significant reduction in the composite endpoint of cardiovascular death and HF-related hospitalizations [20]. A pooled analysis confirmed these functional and clinical benefits across the heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF) spectrum [21]. Extensive meta-analyses and systematic reviews, including Cochrane reviews, have further consolidated these findings, highlighting consistent improvements in quality of life (measured by the Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire) and exercise capacity [22,23,24].

## Real-World Registries, Safety, and Clinical Integration

Real-world registry data have confirmed the long-term safety, durability, and survival benefits of CCM therapy outside of clinical trial cohorts [25,26]. Observational data from the CCM-REG registry demonstrated that patients treated with CCM achieved survival rates that met or exceeded those predicted by standard mortality risk models [25]. 

Furthermore, clinical experience has shown that CCM can be safely co-implanted with implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) [27,28]. There is no evidence of adverse electrical interactions, signal cross-talk, or inappropriate ICD sensing [27,28]. CCM has also demonstrated efficacy in special HF populations, such as patients who have failed to respond to CRT [29] and patients presenting with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) [30].

Based on this evidence, major international clinical guidelines have incorporated CCM. The 2021 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Guidelines recommend considering CCM in selected patients with symptomatic HF (NYHA III–IV, LVEF 25%–45%, QRS < 120 ms) to improve exercise capacity and quality of life [1]. Similarly, the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guidelines recognize CCM as an appropriate device option for symptomatic HF patients on GDMT who meet these clinical criteria [2].

## Conclusion

Cardiac contractility modulation represents a crucial advancement in device-based heart failure management. By targeting cellular calcium dynamics and encouraging reverse molecular remodeling, CCM provides significant functional, clinical, and quality-of-life benefits for a patient population that was previously ineligible for device therapies. Future directions will focus on optimizing patient selection, exploring long-term mortality benefits, and expanding its application across the broader heart failure spectrum.
